note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/13 An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry/13.2 Characteristic organic reactions.md
outline: Identify the reaction by what changes: addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation or redox. Follow electron movement to classify the mechanism. Homolysis creates radicals; heterolysis creates ions. Nucleophiles donate electron pairs and electrophiles accept them. In a full curly-arrow mechanism, every arrow begins at the source bond or lone pair.

misconceptions.refutation: Each atom receives one bonding electron, forming radicals; heterolytic fission produces ions.
misconceptions.contrast: Homolytic: one electron each. Heterolytic: both electrons to one atom.

misconceptions.refutation: A neutral molecule with a lone pair, such as ammonia, can donate that pair.
misconceptions.contrast: Electron-pair donation defines a nucleophile, not charge.

misconceptions.statement: A curly arrow can start at an electrophilic atom.
misconceptions.refutation: A full curly arrow traces an electron pair from its source: a bond or lone pair.
misconceptions.contrast: Start at the electron pair and point towards its destination.

misconceptions.statement: Cyanide addition to a carbonyl first makes a positive carbonyl intermediate.
misconceptions.refutation: The carbon nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon while the C=O pair moves to oxygen, giving an alkoxide.
misconceptions.contrast: Show the C=O polarity and arrows from the cyanide lone pair and C=O bond.

misconceptions.statement: Removing water from an alcohol to form an alkene is hydrolysis or substitution.
misconceptions.refutation: This is elimination: atoms are removed and a carbon–carbon double bond forms. Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond; substitution replaces an atom or group.
misconceptions.contrast: Addition consumes a multiple bond; elimination forms one. Water produced is not water used in hydrolysis.

misconceptions.statement: Every propagation step increases the number of radicals.
misconceptions.refutation: A standard propagation step consumes one radical and produces one radical, maintaining the chain carrier.
misconceptions.contrast: Initiation generates radicals; propagation regenerates the carrier; termination removes radicals.

misconceptions.statement: The protonation arrow starts at the proton and points to negative oxygen.
misconceptions.refutation: The full curly arrow begins at the oxygen lone pair and points to the proton, because oxygen supplies the electron pair.
misconceptions.contrast: Follow the electrons from oxygen to hydrogen, rather than drawing the movement of a proton.

flashcards.back: A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$.
Saturated: contains only carbon–carbon single bonds. Unsaturated: contains a carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
Homolytic: each atom receives one electron from the bond, forming radicals. Heterolytic: one atom receives both bonding electrons, forming ions.
A species with an unpaired electron.
A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts an electron pair.
Addition combines reactants into one product; substitution replaces an atom or group; elimination removes atoms or groups, usually forming a multiple bond.
Hydrolysis breaks a bond by reaction with water. Condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule, often water.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. $[O]$ and $[H]$ each represent one atom supplied by the appropriate reagent.

9701-13.2.1.motivate: Reaction names become useful when they tell you exactly what changes in bonds or electrons. The same short vocabulary works across the organic syllabus.
9701-13.2.1.establish: A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$. Saturated compounds have only carbon–carbon single bonds; unsaturated compounds have a carbon–carbon multiple bond. Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each atom, forming free radicals with unpaired electrons. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one atom, forming ions. Radical initiation generates radicals, propagation consumes and regenerates radicals, and termination removes radicals by combination. A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts one. Addition combines reactants into one product; substitution replaces an atom or group; elimination removes atoms or groups, often forming a multiple bond. Hydrolysis breaks a bond using water; condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule. Organic oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, and reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. $[O]$ and $[H]$ represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent and one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent, respectively.
9701-13.2.1.connect: Electron-pair donors are nucleophiles; electron-pair acceptors are electrophiles. This links the reaction labels here to the four mechanism types in the next idea.
9701-13.2.1.note:
- Homolysis → radicals; heterolysis → ions.
- Initiation creates, propagation sustains, termination removes radicals.
- Addition joins; substitution replaces; elimination removes.
- Hydrolysis uses water; condensation loses a small molecule.
- Oxidation gains O or loses H; reduction loses O or gains H.
9701-13.2.1.self_explain: Why can a neutral molecule be a nucleophile, and how would you distinguish homolytic from heterolytic fission in an electron diagram?

9701-13.2.1.plain_words: First ask what changes: bonds, atoms or electron ownership. A covalent bond holds two electrons. Sharing out one each makes radicals; keeping the pair together on one atom makes ions. Reaction labels describe the overall change, whereas chain-stage labels describe what happens to radicals.
9701-13.2.1.prerequisite_bridge: Recall covalent bonding: count the two bonding electrons before and after a bond breaks. Recall redox: electron loss is oxidation and electron gain is reduction; for organic structures compare oxygen and hydrogen content of the organic molecule. For example, turning ethanol into ethanal removes two hydrogen atoms and is oxidation.

forms.name: Allocate electrons in bond fission
wordings: Describe the fate of the bonding electrons.
Deduce whether ions or radicals form.
forms.example: 1. Start with the two electrons in $\ce{Cl-Cl}$. 2. In homolysis one goes to each Cl, giving $\ce{2Cl.}$, with no ionic charges. 3. Contrast heterolysis of $\ce{H-Cl}$ toward Cl: both electrons go to Cl, giving $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$. 4. Check that two electrons have been allocated and total charge remains zero.
forms.check: Describe the products and electron allocation when $\ce{Br-Br}$ undergoes homolytic fission. Contrast this with heterolytic fission of $\ce{CH3-Br}$ when the bonding pair goes to Br.
forms.answer: Homolysis gives $\ce{2Br.}$, each receiving one bonding electron. Heterolysis gives $\ce{CH3+ + Br-}$, with both bonding electrons on Br. Each process conserves the bonding pair and total charge.

rubric.point: Homolysis of Br–Br forms two bromine radicals (2Br· or Br· + Br·), each receiving one of the two bonding electrons. Require bromine identity, two radicals, and one bonding electron to each; accept equivalent radical drawings and wording. An unspecified radical or a different radical is insufficient, even if matching words occur elsewhere in the heterolysis answer.
Heterolysis forms methyl cation and bromide, both bonding electrons to Br. Accept equivalent displayed charged structures.

retry.check: An isolated $\ce{H-Br}$ bond is broken in two hypothetical ways: one electron to each atom, or both electrons to Br. Name each fission and give the species formed.
retry.answer: One each: homolytic fission, $\ce{H. + Br.}$. Both to Br: heterolytic fission, $\ce{H+ + Br-}$. The radical dot and ionic charge describe different electron arrangements.

rubric.point: One each is homolytic, giving hydrogen and bromine radicals.
Both to Br is heterolytic, giving a proton and bromide. Accept equivalent correctly displayed ionic structures.

forms.name: Identify radical chain stages
forms.example: 1. $\ce{Cl2 ->[UV] 2Cl.}$ starts the chain: initiation. 2. $\ce{Cl. + CH4 -> HCl + CH3.}$ consumes one radical and makes one: propagation. 3. $\ce{CH3. + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl.}$ regenerates the chain carrier: propagation. 4. $\ce{CH3. + CH3. -> C2H6}$ removes two radicals: termination. Count radicals rather than guessing from the product name.
forms.check: Classify each step and justify with radical counts: (i) $\ce{Br2 ->[UV] 2Br.}$; (ii) $\ce{Br. + C2H6 -> HBr + C2H5.}$; (iii) $\ce{C2H5. + Br. -> C2H5Br}$.
forms.answer: Initiation: zero to two radicals. Propagation: one radical consumed and one produced. Termination: two radicals combine and no radical remains.

rubric.point: First step is initiation because radicals are generated from a molecule.
Second is propagation because a radical is regenerated.
Third is termination because two radicals combine without a radical product.

retry.check: Classify and explain: (i) $\ce{C2H5. + Cl2 -> C2H5Cl + Cl.}$; (ii) $\ce{Cl. + Cl. -> Cl2}$; (iii) $\ce{CH3Cl ->[UV] CH3. + Cl.}$.
retry.answer: The first is propagation (one radical to one). The second is termination (two radicals to zero). The third is initiation (a non-radical molecule forms radicals by homolytic fission).

rubric.point: First is propagation with radical regeneration.
Second is termination with radical removal.
Third is initiation by homolysis.

forms.name: Classify overall reaction changes
wordings: Identify the reaction type and explain what changes.
Distinguish hydrolysis from elimination or condensation.
forms.example: 1. $\ce{CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3CH3}$ is addition because two reactants give one product across a double bond; it is also reduction because hydrogen is gained. 2. $\ce{CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br-}$ is substitution because OH replaces Br; with aqueous hydroxide it is also hydrolysis. 3. $\ce{CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O}$ is elimination: water leaves a single organic molecule. 4. Ethanoic acid and ethanol joining to make ethyl ethanoate and water is condensation. Labels can overlap when they describe different aspects.
forms.check: Identify and justify the changes: (i) propan-2-ol to propene plus water; (ii) propanal plus $2[H]$ to propan-1-ol; (iii) methyl ethanoate plus water to ethanoic acid and methanol. State what $[H]$ represents.
forms.answer: The first is elimination: water is removed and a carbon–carbon double bond forms. The second is reduction: the aldehyde gains hydrogen; [H] means one hydrogen atom supplied by a reducing agent. The third is hydrolysis: water breaks the ester linkage.

rubric.point: First is elimination with water loss and double-bond formation.
Second is reduction by hydrogen gain; [H] is one atom from a reducing agent.
Third is hydrolysis because water breaks the ester bond. Accept water splitting the ester linkage.

retry.check: Classify and justify: (i) propan-1-ol plus $[O]$ to propanal plus water; (ii) propene plus bromine to 1,2-dibromopropane; (iii) methanoic acid plus propan-1-ol to propyl methanoate plus water. State what $[O]$ represents.
retry.answer: The first is oxidation by loss of hydrogen from the alcohol; [O] represents one oxygen atom supplied by an oxidising agent. The second is addition across the carbon–carbon double bond. The third is condensation: two organic molecules join and water is lost.

rubric.point: Oxidation removes hydrogen from propan-1-ol; [O] denotes one oxygen atom supplied by an oxidising agent, not an oxygen molecule. Accept a single atom, 1 atom or one atom, and oxidising/oxidizing agent. An explicit claim that [O] means O2 or an oxygen molecule does not earn this point, even if other keywords occur.
Second is addition across the double bond.
Third is condensation with joining and water loss.

forms.name: Apply organic vocabulary to structures and species
wordings: Explain whether compounds belong to the same homologous series.
Identify a nucleophile or electrophile from electron-pair behaviour.
forms.example: 1. Ethanol and propan-1-ol have the alcohol functional group and differ by $\ce{CH2}$: the same homologous series. 2. Ethene has $\ce{C=C}$, so is unsaturated. 3. Ammonia can donate its nitrogen lone pair, so is a neutral nucleophile. 4. $\ce{H+}$ accepts that pair, so acts as an electrophile. Use electron-pair roles rather than charge alone.
forms.check: Compare butane and pentane as homologues and state whether they are saturated. Explain the role of $\ce{H2O}$ when its oxygen donates a lone pair to $\ce{H+}$, and identify the role of $\ce{H+}$.
forms.answer: Butane and pentane are saturated alkanes: only carbon–carbon single bonds, the same general formula $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$, and neighbouring members differing by $\ce{CH2}$. Water is the nucleophile because it donates an electron pair; the proton is the electrophile because it accepts the pair.

rubric.point: Same alkane series and adjacent members differ by CH2.
Saturated because there is no carbon–carbon multiple bond.
Water donates and proton accepts the electron pair.

retry.check: Explain whether ethene and propene are homologues and whether they are saturated. In a bond-forming step $\ce{OH-}$ donates an oxygen lone pair to an electron-deficient carbon; identify the electron-pair roles of both partners.
retry.answer: Ethene and propene are unsaturated alkenes with the same general formula $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}}$; they differ by $\ce{CH2}$. Hydroxide is the nucleophile; the electron-deficient carbon is the electrophilic centre accepting the pair.

rubric.point: Same alkene series; CH2 difference.
Unsaturated because each contains a carbon–carbon double bond.
Hydroxide donates as nucleophile; carbon accepts as electrophilic centre.

misconceptions.idea: Homolytic fission produces ions rather than radicals.
misconceptions.temptation: Both radicals and ions are reactive, so their symbols seem interchangeable.
misconceptions.fix: Count the bonding electrons: one each gives unpaired electrons and radical dots; both to one gives the charge separation in these neutral bond-fission examples.

misconceptions.idea: Propagation increases the radical count at every step.
misconceptions.temptation: A chain grows, so there should be more radicals after each reaction.
misconceptions.fix: Each standard propagation step consumes one radical and forms one; the chain continues because the carrier is regenerated.

misconceptions.idea: Water among the products always means hydrolysis.
misconceptions.temptation: The word hydrolysis suggests any reaction involving water.
misconceptions.fix: Check its role: hydrolysis consumes water to split a bond; elimination can produce water from one organic molecule, and condensation joins molecules while losing water.

9701-13.2.2.motivate: A mechanism explains a reaction at electron level. Its name predicts both the attacking species and the overall bond change.
9701-13.2.2.establish: Free-radical substitution replaces an atom through radical initiation, propagation and termination; alkane chlorination under UV light is an example. Electrophilic addition begins when an alkene π bond donates a pair to an electrophile; addition across $\ce{C=C}$ follows. Nucleophilic substitution begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to a carbon attached to a leaving group, which departs; cyanide replacing bromide is an example. Nucleophilic addition begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to the partially positive carbonyl carbon; the $\ce{C=O}$ pair moves to oxygen, and the alkoxide can then be protonated. Full curly arrows represent movement of electron pairs, so each arrow must start at the source bond or lone pair and point to the destination. Show relevant bond polarity and charges. A radical step instead transfers single electrons and uses single-headed arrows when drawn.
9701-13.2.2.connect: Use the terminology from the first idea to identify electron donors and acceptors, then ask whether the overall change is addition or substitution.
9701-13.2.2.note:
- Radical substitution: initiation, propagation, termination.
- Electrophilic addition: alkene π bond attacks electrophile.
- Nucleophilic substitution: lone-pair donor replaces leaving group.
- Nucleophilic addition: donor attacks carbonyl carbon; $\ce{C=O}$ pair moves to oxygen.
- Full curly arrows start at a bond or lone pair.
9701-13.2.2.self_explain: In cyanide addition to a carbonyl, where do the two full curly arrows begin, and why is the mechanism nucleophilic addition?

discover.stem: Where must a full curly arrow begin?

options.A: At the atom receiving an electron pair.
options.C: At a bond or lone pair supplying the electron pair.
options.D: At the centre of the molecule.

discover.explanation: The tail identifies the electron-pair source; the head shows where the pair moves.

9701-13.2.2.plain_words: Use two decisions: who supplies the electron pair, and what changes overall? An alkene donates its bond pair to an electrophile in electrophilic addition. A nucleophile donates a lone pair: replacing a leaving group is substitution, whereas opening a carbonyl double bond is addition. Every full curly arrow follows a pair from its source.
9701-13.2.2.prerequisite_bridge: From covalent and dative bonding, recall that a bond forms when two atoms share an electron pair, and a donor can supply both electrons. From bond polarity, oxygen and halogens draw bonding electrons toward themselves, making their bonded carbon electron-deficient. Use the reaction labels from the first card only after comparing reactant and product bonds.

forms.name: Classify mechanisms from attacker and bond change
wordings: Name the mechanism and justify both parts of its name.
Distinguish nucleophilic substitution from nucleophilic addition.
forms.example: 1. Ethene plus HBr: the alkene bond pair goes to an electrophile and atoms add across $\ce{C=C}$, so electrophilic addition. 2. Bromoethane plus cyanide: a lone-pair donor replaces bromide, so nucleophilic substitution. 3. Propanone plus HCN: cyanide supplies a lone pair and the carbonyl opens without a leaving group being replaced, so nucleophilic addition. 4. Methane plus chlorine under UV replaces H by Cl through a radical chain, so free-radical substitution.
forms.check: Name and justify the mechanism in each stated transformation: (i) aqueous hydroxide replaces I in iodomethane; (ii) HCl adds across the double bond in but-2-ene; (iii) cyanide adds to pentan-2-one followed by protonation.
forms.answer: The first is nucleophilic substitution: hydroxide donates a lone pair and iodide leaves. The second is electrophilic addition: the alkene supplies its pi pair to electrophilic hydrogen, and H and Cl add across the double bond. The third is nucleophilic addition: cyanide donates a carbon lone pair to the carbonyl carbon without replacement of a leaving group.

rubric.point: First is nucleophilic substitution with donor and leaving group identified.

Electrophilic addition: the alkene pi electron pair attacks/ is donated to electrophilic H of the hydrogen halide, and H and halogen add across C=C. Accept equivalent prose or correctly directed arrows; a mechanism name plus bond label alone is insufficient. Accept the electron-rich C=C or double bond attacking electrophilic H followed by halide addition, without explicitly saying electron pair.

Nucleophilic addition: cyanide attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated; alternatively describe carbon lone-pair donation and addition across C=O. Explicit electron-pair and no-replacement wording is not required for the attack-and-protonation explanation. A mechanism name plus carbonyl label alone is insufficient; accept equivalent correctly directed arrows.

retry.check: Name and justify: (i) HBr adds to cyclohexene; (ii) cyanide adds to butanal and the alkoxide is protonated; (iii) ammonia replaces Br in 1-bromopropane.
retry.answer: (i) Electrophilic addition: the cyclohexene C=C pi electron pair attacks the electrophilic H of HBr; H and Br add across the double bond. (ii) Nucleophilic addition: cyanide donates its carbon lone pair to the carbonyl carbon of butanal, moving the C=O pi pair onto oxygen; protonation of the alkoxide gives the hydroxynitrile, with no leaving group replaced. (iii) Nucleophilic substitution: ammonia donates its nitrogen lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br, replacing the bromide leaving group.

rubric.point: Electrophilic addition: the alkene pi electron pair attacks/ is donated to electrophilic H of the hydrogen halide, and H and halogen add across C=C. Accept equivalent prose or correctly directed arrows; a mechanism name plus bond label alone is insufficient. Accept C=C attacking electrophilic H followed by addition across the double bond without explicitly saying electron pair.

Nucleophilic addition: cyanide attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated; alternatively describe carbon lone-pair donation and addition across C=O. Explicit electron-pair and no-replacement wording is not required for the attack-and-protonation explanation. A mechanism name plus carbonyl label alone is insufficient; accept equivalent correctly directed arrows.
Ammonia is a lone-pair donor in nucleophilic substitution.

forms.name: Describe alkene–hydrogen halide curly arrows
wordings: Describe the mechanism including arrow origins and intermediate.
Explain why an arrow must start at the alkene bond.
forms.example: Worked example: ethene plus HCl. 1. Show H in H–Cl as $\delta^+$ and Cl as $\delta^-$. Draw a full curly arrow from the middle of the alkene pi bond to H, while another runs from the H–Cl bond to Cl. 2. One carbon gains H; the other is the positively charged carbon in $\ce{CH3CH2+}$, accompanied by $\ce{Cl-}$. 3. Draw a full curly arrow from a chloride lone pair to that positive carbon, giving chloroethane. 4. Check: every arrow starts at a pair, carbon valencies are valid, and total charge is conserved.
forms.check: Describe the full mechanism for HBr addition to symmetrical but-2-ene, including the two first-stage arrows, intermediate charge and final arrow.
forms.answer: Show $\ce{H^{\delta+}-Br^{\delta-}}$. An arrow runs from the $\ce{C=C}$ pi bond to H; simultaneously one runs from H–Br to Br. The intermediate is the secondary carbocation $\ce{CH3CH2CH+CH3}$ plus bromide. An arrow from a bromide lone pair to the positively charged carbon forms 2-bromobutane. Either equivalent orientation is valid.

rubric.point: First-stage full curly arrow runs from the alkene pi bond to H of HBr.
Second arrow runs from H–Br bond to Br.

Correct secondary carbocation and bromide, then bromide lone pair to positive carbon gives 2-bromobutane. Accept CH3CH+CH2CH3 or CH3CH2CH+CH3 and equivalent charged drawings; accept any correct displayed or structural formula of 2-bromobutane in either chain orientation, without requiring a particular stereoisomer. Accept equivalent displayed charged structures in either chain orientation without requiring the word carbocation.

retry.check: Describe HCl addition to cyclohexene: give the first-stage arrow tails and heads, the intermediate charges, and the final electron-pair movement. Name the organic product.
retry.answer: The alkene pi-bond arrow points to the partially positive H of HCl; the H–Cl bond arrow points to Cl. This gives a cyclohexyl carbocation and chloride. A chloride lone pair donates to the positive carbon, forming chlorocyclohexane.

rubric.point: Pi bond to H; H–Cl bond to Cl.

Require the cyclohexyl carbocation (also called cyclohexyl cation or cyclohexan-1-yl cation), with the positive charge on a former alkene carbon, and chloride; accept equivalent correctly charged ring drawings.

Chloride lone pair to positive carbon forms chlorocyclohexane. Accept 1-chlorocyclohexane or an equivalent displayed/skeletal saturated six-carbon ring with one Cl substituent; the chloride lone-pair arrow must end at the positively charged carbon.

misconceptions.idea: Start an arrow at the species being attacked.
misconceptions.temptation: The reaction is described as attack on an atom, so that atom seems the natural starting point.
misconceptions.fix: The tail locates the electron pair: use the alkene bond, a nucleophile lone pair or the bond being broken. The head gives its destination.

misconceptions.idea: A carbonyl first loses oxygen to form a positive carbon intermediate.
misconceptions.temptation: The carbonyl carbon is partially positive, which can be mistaken for a carbocation.
misconceptions.fix: Carbonyl addition moves the pi pair onto oxygen while a new carbon–carbon bond forms. Oxygen remains bonded and carries the negative charge in the alkoxide.

misconceptions.idea: Draw protonation from the proton to oxygen.
misconceptions.temptation: Hydrogen is joining the molecule, so its movement seems to determine arrow direction.
misconceptions.fix: Curly arrows track electrons, not atoms. The electron pair begins on oxygen and ends at hydrogen.

misconceptions.idea: All nucleophiles are negative and attack double bonds.
misconceptions.temptation: Cyanide and hydroxide are familiar negative ions.
misconceptions.fix: Neutral ammonia is also a donor. In substitution the donor attacks a carbon bonded to a leaving group; a double bond is not required.
